The parthenogenetic lizard Darevskia unisexualis, a unisexual species of hybrid origin, exhibits a series of life-history traits that reflect its clonal reproductive mode. Neonates emerge with a snout-vent length of approximately 2.25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.25 centimeters], a value comparable to hatchling sizes observed in the related bisexual species Darevskia derjugini. This modest size at hatching is typical of the genus, and juveniles grow steadily as they exploit the rock crevice habitats characteristic of the Caucasus region. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded reproductive rate of these females is the product of a small but consistent clutch size. Females typically deposit 8 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = 8 eggs per reproductive event], producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], which yields a theoretical annual output of 8 eggs per year. This modest fecundity, combined with a relatively extended period of growth, shapes the overall demographic strategy of Darevskia unisexualis compared to that of sympatric bisexual congeners.

Body mass parameters in this species provide insight into its energetic allocation patterns during ontogeny. At hatching, the wet body mass of a neonate is about 0.26 grams [Wwb = about 0.26 grams], again based on data extrapolated from Darevskia derjugini, as direct measurements on the unisexual form remain scarce. This initial mass supports the hatchling until it commences exogenous feeding, which occurs within the first few days following emergence from the parchment-shelled egg. The corresponding ultimate or asymptotic wet body mass attained by fully grown adults is considerably larger, with graid females reaching a maximum wet weight of 8.38 grams [Wwi = 8.38 grams]. This nearly 32-fold increase from hatchling to adult mass reflects the substantial somatic investment that precedes the onset of reproductive activity. Such a trajectory is not unusual among small-bodied lacertids, though it implies a protracted growth phase that likely imposes constraints on the timing of first reproduction in this obligate parthenogen.

The maximum lifespan of Darevskia unisexualis under captive, predator-free conditions at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C] provides a framework for interpreting its life-cycle pace. Individuals have been recorded surviving for up to a maximum of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] based on interpolation from related species at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This figure is relatively modest among lacertids of comparable body size, but it aligns with the general pattern for unisexual taxa, which often exhibit reduced lifespans relative to their bisexual progenitors. The longevity estimate is particularly relevant because it sets an upper boundary on the number of annual reproductive events a female can achieve. At a rate of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], an individual that lives to its maximum potential could produce no more than eight clutches in its lifetime, placing a premium on the survival of each clutch and the success of each hatchling cohort in the subsequent generation.

Gonadal maturation in this parthenogenetic lizard is characterized by a relatively long juvenile period, during which females accumulate the necessary body reserves for vitellogenesis. Under the same thermal conditions as the lifespan data, specifically at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the typical age at first reproduction is reached at approximately three years after hatching such that the onset of egg laying occurs 3 years after hatching [tR = 3 years after hatching]. This delay is substantial when viewed in proportion to the total 8 year lifespan, meaning nearly 40% of the potential life span elapses before any reproductive output is realized. The prolonged prereproductive phase is likely linked to the high mass-specific investment required to produce the 8 egg clutch, as each egg represents a significant proportion of maternal body mass. This contrasts with some smaller lacertids that mature within one to two years, highlighting a relatively slow life-history strategy for Darevskia unisexualis that may be advantageous for exploiting stable but resource-limited rock outcrop environments.

The ultimate snout-vent length attained by adult females of Darevskia unisexualis has been documented through field measurements of gravid individuals, with the maximum recorded size reaching 6.7 centimeters [Li = 6.7 centimeters]. This dimension serves as the upper asymptote of somatic growth and is broadly consistent with the size at which reproductive allocation becomes energetically favorable. Attaining this ultimate body length requires several growth seasons, and individuals that achieve this size are typically among the oldest in the population, having survived multiple winters. In a comparative context, this maximum SVL is slightly larger than that reported for the bisexual Darevskia derjugini, suggesting that the shift to parthenogenesis in D. unisexualis may be accompanied by a modest increase in adult body size, possibly related to the absence of sexual dimorphism or to direct selection on fecundity. Field surveys indicate that once females reach this asymptotic length, growth plateaus and nearly all available energy is channeled into yolk production and clutch formation, maximizing lifetime reproductive output.
